relationship: same-book renewed prophetic commission
rationale: The opening verse introduces the Lord's word to Jonah. Chapter 3 explicitly says that the word came to him a second time, marking the renewal of this commission after his flight and rescue.

relationship: city's wickedness brought before God
rationale: The Lord sends Jonah to Nineveh because its wickedness has come up before Him. Genesis similarly presents Sodom and Gomorrah's increasing cry and great sins as coming before the Lord ahead of intervention concerning the cities.

relationship: flight from God's presence and the sea
rationale: Jonah boards a ship in an attempt to flee from the Lord's presence. The psalm asks where anyone could flee from God's face and says that even at the sea's farthest reaches His hand remains present.

relationship: the Lord raises a storm at sea
rationale: Jonah's ship is endangered when the Lord stirs up a wind and a great surge arises at sea. The psalm's account of seafarers likewise attributes a storm wind and rising waves to the Lord's command.

relationship: narrative parallel of a sleeper in a storm
rationale: Jonah sleeps below while the sailors fear for their storm-tossed ship. Mark likewise places a sleeping central figure in a boat endangered by a great storm. The comparison concerns the narrative situation; Jonah's flight and Jesus' later command have different roles in their respective stories.

relationship: parallel emergency unloading at sea
rationale: Jonah's sailors throw equipment into the sea to lighten the ship during the storm. Acts describes storm-battered sailors throwing cargo and then the ship's tackle overboard.

relationship: narrative parallel of awakening the sleeper
rationale: The officer calls Jonah to rise from sleep and pray so that those aboard will not perish. Mark's disciples likewise awaken Jesus with a question about their perishing, connecting the awakening with the boat's danger.

relationship: parallel identification of an offender
rationale: The sailors use lots and Jonah is identified as the cause of their trouble. Joshua narrates the successive indication of Judah, a clan and finally Achar in the investigation of Israel's offense. The shared pattern is identification of a particular offender within a larger afflicted group; Joshua's supplied wording says indicated.

relationship: parallel questioning after identification
rationale: After Jonah is identified, the sailors demand an account of the cause of their calamity and his background. Joshua similarly questions the identified Achar, demanding disclosure of what he has done, and receives a confession.

relationship: shared confession of the Lord as creator
rationale: Jonah identifies the God he reveres as the Lord of heaven who made the sea and dry land. Exodus likewise describes the Lord as maker of heaven, earth and sea, explaining the scope of the deity Jonah names while at sea.

relationship: same-chapter progression of the sailors' fear
rationale: The sailors fear greatly and already know of Jonah's flight from the Lord because he had told them. After the sea is calmed, verse 16 again describes their great fear, now explicitly directed to the Lord and expressed in sacrifice and vows.

relationship: same-chapter proposed remedy and narrated outcome
rationale: Jonah says that throwing him into the sea will make it cease raging against the sailors. Verse 15 narrates that action and the sea's resulting cessation, completing the proposal with its stated outcome.

relationship: parallel struggle against hostile waters
rationale: The men strain to return Jonah's ship to land but cannot overcome the sea. Mark describes disciples straining at the rowing because the wind is against them, a corresponding scene of difficult human effort on hostile waters.

relationship: shared prayer against innocent-blood guilt
rationale: The sailors ask the Lord not to lay innocent blood upon them as they prepare to throw Jonah overboard. Deuteronomy provides a communal plea that innocent-blood guilt not remain among the people; both prayers explicitly seek release from that bloodguilt.

relationship: prayer followed by the storm's cessation
rationale: The sea ceases after the sailors' prayer and their action toward Jonah. The psalm likewise narrates seafarers crying to the Lord and the storm being commanded to settle, with the waves falling silent.

relationship: narrative parallel of sudden calm
rationale: Jonah's narrative moves from a raging sea to its cessation when he is thrown overboard. Mark narrates wind ceasing and a great calm after Jesus' command; both episodes emphasize the abrupt end of a dangerous storm, while specifying different actions preceding it.

relationship: sacrifice and vows in response to deliverance
rationale: The sailors offer sacrifice and vows to the Lord after the sea calms. The psalmist likewise promises burnt offerings and payment of vows declared in affliction, joining distress, deliverance and worship.

relationship: fear following the calming of the sea
rationale: Jonah's sailors greatly fear the Lord after the storm ends. Mark's disciples are greatly afraid after Jesus calms the wind and sea and ask who He is, connecting the resulting fear with power over the waters.

relationship: explicit later comparison to Jonah
rationale: Jonah is in the sea creature's belly for three days and three nights. Jesus explicitly cites Jonah's confinement for that duration when comparing it with the Son of Man being in the heart of the earth.

relationship: prayer from mortal danger
rationale: Jonah prays to the Lord from the sea creature's belly. The psalm describes the dangers of Hades and then a cry for the Lord to rescue the speaker's soul, corresponding to prayer from the peril described by Jonah's surrounding narrative and prayer.

relationship: shared prayer language of affliction and Hades
rationale: Jonah recalls crying in affliction and being heard from the belly of Hades. The psalm likewise joins Hades, affliction, crying to God and God's hearing of the voice from His holy temple.

relationship: shared billows-and-waves prayer language
rationale: Jonah says that all God's billows and waves passed over him in the sea's depth. The psalm uses the same combination of God's billows and waves passing over the speaker in its language of the deep.

relationship: shared lament of exclusion from God's sight
rationale: Jonah says he has been thrust away from God's eyes and asks about looking again toward the holy sanctuary. The psalm similarly recalls the alarmed claim of being cast away from God's eyes, followed by acknowledgment that God heard the petition.

relationship: shared imagery of overwhelming waters
rationale: Jonah describes water poured around him as far as his life and the surrounding abyss. The psalm cries for rescue because waters have reached the soul and the speaker has entered the sea's depths, sharing the imagery of life overwhelmed by water.

relationship: descent toward death and appeal for rising
rationale: Jonah describes descent into a land with eternal bars and asks that the ruin of his life rise up. The psalm credits the Lord with bringing the soul up from Hades and saving it from those descending into a pit. The connection is descent toward death and divine rescue; Jonah's supplied petition is preserved as a petition.

relationship: prayer reaching God's holy temple
rationale: Jonah remembers the Lord as his life fails and says his prayer may come into the holy sanctuary. The psalm describes an afflicted cry heard by God from His holy temple, connecting distress with prayer reaching God's dwelling.

relationship: remembering God when the soul is troubled
rationale: Jonah remembers the Lord when his life is failing. The psalm likewise connects the soul's trouble with remembering God, giving a close parallel to the prayer's movement from distress to remembrance.

relationship: shared rejection of empty vanities
rationale: Jonah says that those guarding vain and false things abandoned their mercy. The psalm also speaks of those guarding vanities to no purpose and contrasts that practice with hope in the Lord.

relationship: sacrifice of praise and payment of vows
rationale: Jonah promises sacrifice with praise and thanksgiving and payment of his vows. The psalm explicitly commands a sacrifice of praise and payment of vows, followed by the promise of rescue when God is called upon in affliction.

relationship: deliverance belongs to the Lord
rationale: Jonah closes his promise of worship with deliverance directed to the Lord. The psalm directly declares that salvation belongs to the Lord, matching the prayer's attribution of rescue to Him.

relationship: same-chapter commands framing confinement
rationale: The Lord first commands the sea creature to swallow Jonah. Later the creature is commanded, and it casts him onto dry land; the later command's content is unstated. The two reported commands frame his confinement and release.

relationship: same-book renewed prophetic commission
rationale: The Lord's word comes to Jonah a second time here. The opening verse records the first coming of that word, so the repeated introduction explicitly marks the renewed commission.

relationship: same-book renewed commission to Nineveh
rationale: The renewed command sends Jonah to Nineveh and expressly refers to the former proclamation. The opening command names the same city and charges him to proclaim there because its wickedness has come before God.

relationship: same-book reversal from flight to obedience
rationale: Jonah now rises and goes to Nineveh according to the Lord's word. Earlier he rose to flee to Tarshish from the Lord's presence; the two departures contrast resistance with obedience to the commission.

relationship: explicit later reference to Jonah's proclamation
rationale: Jonah's recorded proclamation warns that Nineveh will be overthrown in three more days in this source edition. Matthew explicitly refers to the Ninevites repenting at Jonah's proclamation, identifying the preaching whose effect the narrative records.

relationship: explicit later reference to Nineveh's repentance
rationale: Nineveh's people believe God and proclaim a fast with sackcloth. Matthew explicitly describes the men of Nineveh as having repented at Jonah's proclamation and makes their response a witness at the judgment.

relationship: fasting joined to turning toward God
rationale: Nineveh's people respond to the divine warning with belief, fasting and sackcloth. Joel calls for turning to the Lord with fasting and wholehearted repentance, connecting the outward fast with the response to God.

relationship: parallel royal humbling after a prophetic warning
rationale: Nineveh's king leaves his throne and royal clothing and puts on sackcloth upon hearing the message. Ahab likewise responds to the prophetic word by weeping, tearing his tunic, wearing sackcloth and fasting, after which the Lord acknowledges his humbling.

relationship: parallel communal abstention from food and drink
rationale: Nineveh's royal decree forbids food and water for the people and livestock. Esther similarly commands the gathered Jews in Susa to fast without eating or drinking. The shared feature is a publicly directed fast with both food and drink withheld; Nineveh's decree additionally includes livestock.

relationship: fasting accompanied by rejection of injustice
rationale: Nineveh's response joins sackcloth and crying to God with each person turning from evil and the injustice in their hands. Isaiah likewise says that sackcloth and outward fasting are inadequate and calls instead for releasing people from injustice and caring for the vulnerable.

relationship: shared hope that God may relent
rationale: Nineveh's people ask who knows whether God will relent and turn from wrath so they do not perish. Joel likewise asks who knows whether He will turn and relent, expressing hope rather than assuming the outcome.

relationship: narrative example of conditional judgment
rationale: God sees Nineveh turn from evil and does not bring the announced calamity. Jeremiah explicitly states that when a threatened nation turns from its evils, the Lord will change His mind concerning the destruction He planned.

relationship: narrative analogy of resentment at mercy
rationale: Jonah is grieved after Nineveh is spared, and his following prayer names God's mercy as the issue. The older son likewise objects when his father welcomes the returning son, and the father explains why restoration calls for joy. The relationship is a shared response of resentment at mercy extended to another.

relationship: shared declaration of God's merciful character
rationale: Jonah describes God as merciful, compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy when explaining his flight. Exodus's proclamation of the Lord's name uses the same cluster of merciful attributes.

relationship: shared mercy and relenting formula
rationale: Jonah explains that he knew God was merciful, compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy and one who relents concerning calamities. Joel uses that same sequence of attributes to ground the appeal to turn to the Lord.

relationship: parallel prophet's request for death
rationale: Jonah asks the Lord to take his life because death seems better to him. Elijah likewise asks the Lord to take his life during his distressed withdrawal, giving a close parallel between the two prophets' death wishes.

relationship: same-chapter repeated question about grief
rationale: The Lord first asks whether Jonah is deeply grieved after Nineveh is spared. The question recurs with the gourd named explicitly in verse 9, drawing Jonah's reaction to the city and his reaction to the plant into comparison.

relationship: divine shelter from the sun
rationale: God provides the gourd to shade Jonah's head and shelter him. The psalm describes the Lord as a shelter and promises that the sun will not scorch the one He guards, corresponding to the protection the plant gives before its removal.

relationship: same-book motif of commanded creatures
rationale: God commands a worm that strikes Jonah's protective gourd. Earlier He commanded the sea creature to swallow Jonah. Both episodes show a creature changing the prophet's circumstances under divine command, within the book's larger contrast with Jonah's initial flight from his own command.

relationship: same-book motif of divinely sent winds
rationale: God commands a scorching wind on land, and the text then reports the sun striking Jonah's head. Earlier the Lord stirred up a wind at sea, explicitly followed by a great surge. Both episodes feature divinely directed winds, while describing their accompanying events differently.

relationship: same-chapter repeated question about grief
rationale: The Lord asks about Jonah's deep grief over the gourd, repeating the earlier question after the city's deliverance. The repetition prepares the comparison between the plant Jonah values and Nineveh's people and livestock.

relationship: same-chapter lesser-to-greater compassion argument
rationale: The Lord points to Jonah sparing a brief-lived gourd for which he had not labored. The next question applies that concern to the far greater case of Nineveh with its many people and livestock, completing the argument about compassion.

relationship: divine compassion extending across God's works
rationale: The Lord's question includes both Nineveh's numerous people and its livestock in the reason for sparing the city. The psalm describes the Lord as merciful and His compassions as extending over all His works, corresponding to the breadth of that concern.

relationship: parallel divine questions about sparing a people
rationale: The Lord asks whether He should not spare Nineveh. Hosea similarly presents God's questions about how to deal with Ephraim and His refusal to act according to furious anger or erase them. The populations differ, but both speeches make divine compassion central to withholding destruction.
